content: The HIV cascade of services is depicted as a comprehensive framework, but individual pathways through it may differ. While prevention is illustrated as the initial step, opportunities for prevention also arise at every subsequent stage, including during testing and counseling for both HIV-negative and HIV-positive individuals, as well as throughout HIV care and treatment for those who test positive. The quality of prevention efforts directly impacts HIV incidence and is critical to achieving the goal of ending AIDS. Strategic information is essential for understanding the epidemic. This involves analyzing patterns by key populations, age, sex, and location. Inputs include health system resources and financing, while outputs refer to activities and their results, such as the number of people tested, enrolled in care, or receiving treatment. Outcomes measure the shortand medium-term effects of these outputs, such as service coverage and viral suppression rates. Ultimately, the impact is evaluated by reductions in HIV incidence and mortality, as well as improvements in equity. Prevention remains a key focus at all stages of the cascade. It is not limited to the initial step but is integrated throughout the continuum of care. Effective prevention strategies are vital for reducing new infections and achieving global AIDS targets. The prioritization of indicators is a central aim of this guidance. By focusing on fewer, high-quality indicators, efforts can be directed toward improving data collection, disaggregation, analysis, and use. This approach enhances program performance along the cascade of prevention, care, and treatment. Information systems must prioritize the most useful indicators to support better services. Consistently collected, fully disaggregated, and well-analyzed indicators are more effective than a large number of poorly collected and underutilized ones. The document emphasizes the importance of tested indicators that are relevant for HIV program management and reporting at sub-national, national, and global levels. WHO is leading efforts to establish a consolidated set of 100 key health indicators, including those for HIV. These indicators aim to harmonize reporting requirements, improve alignment between global monitoring needs and country processes, and enhance the quality of results-based monitoring. Data disaggregation is crucial for ensuring that services reach those in need and that no one is left behind. Disaggregating data by age, sex, key populations, location, and other factors allows for targeted responses and highlights disparities. This approach informs sub-national and local responses, aligning with the post-2015 development agenda. HIV-related data are typically disaggregated by age (using standard age groups), sex, key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, prisoners, sex workers, transgender individuals), location, and pregnancy or breastfeeding status. Confidentiality and security are critical when collecting and analyzing data from key populations. The guidance categorizes indicators into three groups: national, global, and additional. National program indicators (50 in total) provide a comprehensive overview of the HIV epidemic and response. These indicators should be included in national monitoring systems, tailored to the country context. Global indicators (10 in total) are selected from the national set to provide an overview of the health sector response and to track trends in program performance. Additional indicators may be used at the national or sub-national level to address specific needs. Investing in data systems is essential for tracking these indicators. Allocating 5–10% of overall program funds to data collection and analysis is recommended. Key data sources include facility and outreach reporting systems, administrative data, population-based surveys, facility assessments, and vital registration systems. The 10 global indicators recommended by WHO focus on key aspects of the health sector response, such as HIV prevalence, domestic financing, HIV care, ART retention, viral suppression, AIDS-related deaths, and new infections. These indicators are aligned with the 90–90–90 treatment targets and aim to standardize accountability at the global level. They provide essential information for identifying gaps, improving programs, and achieving national and global targets. The prioritization and alignment of indicators along the health sector cascade support accountability for the 90–90–90 targets and other goals. This approach ensures that data are used effectively to inform actions, improve programs, and maximize impact.
